apply-80-20-principle.title: Use 80/20 as a Prioritization Hypothesis
apply-80-20-principle.subtitle: Look for concentration, then verify it.
apply-80-20-principle.description: Rank the few inputs most likely to matter, test that ranking against observed results, and revise it instead of treating 80/20 as a law or exact forecast.
apply-80-20-principle.reason: Replace an inherited Pareto article containing pseudo-precise effect sizes, arbitrary work intervals, fabricated observations, and ROI-style claims with a bounded prioritization exercise.
forbidden_public_fragments: Research shows habits can take 21-66 days to form

lifeOsSource.hack: Treat 80/20 as a prompt to look for concentration, not as a promise that exactly 20 parts of input create exactly 80 parts of output.
lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: Define one outcome, list the inputs that could influence it, rank a small number by expected impact and cost, choose one to check, and compare the observed result with your initial ranking. Revise the ranking when the data disagrees.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: Which input actually changed the outcome, what did it cost, and what should move up, down, or out of the priority list?

faq.question: Does the result need to match 80/20 exactly?
faq.answer: No. The ratio is a memorable heuristic for uneven contribution. Your real distribution may be different; inspect it rather than force it to match the label.

intro.html: The 80/20 idea is most useful as a question: is a small part of this system carrying a disproportionate share of the result? It is not a universal ratio. Use it to create a ranking you can challenge with real observations.

sections.title: 1. Name the outcome
sections.html: Choose one observable result and avoid optimizing a proxy unless you can explain why it matters.

sections.title: 2. Rank plausible inputs
sections.html: List the activities, customers, causes, features, channels, or failure modes that could drive the outcome. Rank a small number by expected impact, cost, and confidence. Mark guesses as guesses.

sections.title: 3. Check one priority, then re-rank
sections.html: Choose a reversible action that checks an important item near the top. Decide what you will observe first, compare what happened with the ranking, and update the list.

batch-similar-tasks-planner.title: Batch Similar Tasks When Switching Is the Problem
batch-similar-tasks-planner.subtitle: Group work only when shared setup is the bottleneck.
batch-similar-tasks-planner.description: Group comparable low-risk tasks when repeated setup is slowing the work, then compare the batch with your normal flow and stop batching when responsiveness suffers.
batch-similar-tasks-planner.reason: Replace unsupported productivity percentages, invented switching costs, rigid batch durations, and fabricated observations with a reversible workflow exercise.
forbidden_public_fragments: Research shows habits can take 21-66 days to form

lifeOsSource.hack: Batch tasks that use the same tools, information, or decision pattern when repeated setup appears to be the bottleneck.
lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: Pick one recurring task family, define what makes the tasks similar, collect a small batch, process it with the same setup, and record completed items, rework, waiting time, and missed urgency. Compare with the ordinary flow before expanding the batch.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: Did batching remove repeated setup without adding unacceptable delay, rework, or missed urgent work?

faq.question: Should every repetitive task be batched?
faq.answer: No. Batching can add waiting time and hide urgent work. Use it where shared setup matters and where delaying individual items is acceptable.

intro.html: Batching is a workflow option, not a productivity law. It can help when repeated setup dominates the work and hurt when items are urgent, highly variable, or need immediate feedback.

sections.title: 1. Find the repeated setup
sections.html: Identify what you reload or re-decide each time: a system, dataset, template, channel, environment, or rule. If there is little repeated setup, batching may add ceremony without value.

sections.title: 2. Run a small safe batch
sections.html: Collect comparable items and keep urgent, exceptional, or high-risk work outside the batch unless the normal process explicitly supports it.

sections.title: 3. Review the trade-off
sections.html: Keep batching only if it removes friction without damaging responsiveness or quality. Otherwise split the batch or return to one-by-one flow.

adopt-new-tools-at-work.title: Test a New Work Tool on a Reversible Task
adopt-new-tools-at-work.subtitle: Prove the workflow fit before expanding use.
adopt-new-tools-at-work.description: Evaluate a new tool on a low-risk workflow, define the decision criteria first, keep a fallback, and expand only after the observed result justifies the change.
adopt-new-tools-at-work.reason: Replace fabricated pilots, unsupported adoption metrics, medical-adjacent examples, and arbitrary success thresholds with a low-risk tool-evaluation protocol.
forbidden_public_fragments: Research shows habits can take 21-66 days to form

lifeOsSource.hack: Try a new tool on a reversible, noncritical task before changing the wider workflow.
lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: State the problem the tool should solve and the criteria that would justify adoption. Choose a low-risk task, define the current baseline, run the tool with a manual fallback, record errors, effort, output quality and user friction, then decide whether to reject, revise, extend, or adopt.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: What changed versus the current workflow, what failure mode appeared, and is the result strong enough to justify a wider check?

faq.question: Should the first check use safety-critical work?
faq.answer: No. Start with a low-risk reversible case. Safety-critical, legal, financial, security-sensitive, regulated, or care-related workflows need the relevant approval, validation, and expert process.

intro.html: A new tool earns its place by improving a real workflow under its actual constraints. Start with a reversible check, preserve the fallback, and let observed trade-offs determine whether use expands.

sections.title: 1. Define the job and criteria
sections.html: Write the problem in workflow terms. Specify what would have to improve and what must not degrade, including security, privacy, quality, audit, and compliance constraints where relevant.

sections.title: 2. Choose a low-risk case
sections.html: Select work that is representative enough to teach you something but cheap to reverse. Keep the existing method available so the check cannot silently become a forced migration.

sections.title: 3. Observe the full trade-off
sections.html: Record output quality, errors, operator effort, handoffs, reliability, exceptions, checking, and repair time. Expand only when the result meets the criteria and important failure modes have owners.

ai-question-bank-builder.title: Build an AI-Assisted Question Bank You Can Verify
ai-question-bank-builder.subtitle: Let AI draft; let the source decide the answer.
ai-question-bank-builder.description: Use AI to draft varied practice questions from material you already have, verify every answer against the source, and keep only questions that test the knowledge you actually need.
ai-question-bank-builder.reason: Replace unsupported learning-effect percentages, rigid question ratios, fixed timing prescriptions, and research-sounding claims with a source-checked question-authoring workflow.
forbidden_public_fragments: Research shows habits can take 21-66 days to form

lifeOsSource.hack: Use AI as a question drafter, not as the authority for the answer.
lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: Choose a source you need to learn, ask AI for questions covering definitions, explanations, comparisons, application and error cases, verify every answer against the source, remove ambiguous or unsupported items, and practice from the cleaned bank.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: Which questions exposed a gap, which answers could not be verified, and what should be corrected or added before the next practice round?

faq.question: Can the generated answer key be trusted automatically?
faq.answer: No. Check each answer against the source material or another authoritative reference before using it as a learning key.

intro.html: AI can cheaply produce many questions, which makes verification more important, not less. Separate generation from answer authority: draft broadly, check against the source, then practice only from the cleaned set.

sections.title: 1. Anchor the bank to a source
sections.html: Select the notes, manual, textbook section, specification, or other material you actually need to learn. State the scope so questions do not drift into adjacent facts.

sections.title: 2. Vary the questions
sections.html: Include recall, explanation, comparison, application, examples, counterexamples, and common-error checks when those formats fit the material.

sections.title: 3. Verify and edit
sections.html: Check each answer against the source. Delete items that depend on missing context or an answer you cannot verify, and rewrite ambiguous wording before keeping the item.

break-big-goals-into-steps.title: Turn a Large Goal into the Next Verifiable Step
break-big-goals-into-steps.subtitle: Make the finish condition and dependencies visible.
break-big-goals-into-steps.description: Define the finish condition, expose dependencies, split the goal into observable deliverables, and choose the smallest next step that creates information or progress.
break-big-goals-into-steps.reason: Replace unsupported completion-rate claims, fabricated experiments, arbitrary duration rules, and broad motivational promises with a concrete decomposition protocol.
forbidden_public_fragments: Research shows habits can take 21-66 days to form

lifeOsSource.hack: Replace a vague large goal with a visible finish condition, a dependency map, and one next deliverable small enough to start.
lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: Write what done looks like, list the major deliverables and external dependencies, split uncertain work until each next step has an observable output, choose the smallest useful step, complete it, and update the map from what you learned.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: What became complete or clearer, what dependency blocks the next step, and what is the smallest observable deliverable now?

faq.question: Should every future step be planned before starting?
faq.answer: No. Map enough to see the finish condition, major dependencies, and next useful action. Update the decomposition as new information changes the plan.

intro.html: Large goals often hide unclear finish conditions, dependencies, unknowns, and tasks that are still too broad to begin. Decomposition makes those boundaries visible without pretending the first plan will remain correct.

sections.title: 1. Define what done means
sections.html: Write one observable finish condition. Replace labels such as improve the site with a result someone could inspect, check, approve, publish, or use.

sections.title: 2. Map deliverables and dependencies
sections.html: List the few outputs required for the finish condition and mark what depends on another person, decision, system, or unknown.

sections.title: 3. Choose the next verifiable step
sections.html: Break broad work into a deliverable or learning step with a visible result. Complete it, then revise the map and choose the next useful deliverable.

break-down-big-problems-triz.title: Decompose a Hard Problem with TRIZ-Inspired Contradictions
break-down-big-problems-triz.subtitle: Expose the conflict before optimizing around it.
break-down-big-problems-triz.description: Describe the unwanted result, expose the trade-off or contradiction, split the system into parts, and check a change that removes a constraint instead of merely optimizing around it.
break-down-big-problems-triz.reason: Replace pseudo-quantified TRIZ outcomes, fabricated pilots, arbitrary timing rules, and broad superiority claims with a bounded problem-structuring exercise inspired by contradiction and separation.
forbidden_public_fragments: Research shows habits can take 21-66 days to form

lifeOsSource.hack: When a problem resists ordinary optimization, write the contradiction explicitly and look for a way to separate the conflicting requirements by time, place, condition, component, or role.
lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: State the unwanted outcome, map the main parts and interactions, write the trade-off as two requirements that appear to conflict, generate separation or redesign options, choose a reversible check, and record which assumption or constraint changed.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: What contradiction did I expose, what separation or redesign did I check, and did it remove the conflict or only move it elsewhere?

faq.question: Is this a complete TRIZ method?
faq.answer: No. This is a practical TRIZ-inspired structuring exercise using contradiction and separation prompts. It does not represent the full TRIZ body of methods or claim a measured effect.

intro.html: Some problems stay hard because the current design treats a trade-off as fixed. A TRIZ-inspired pass asks whether conflicting requirements can be separated or whether the system can be changed so they no longer compete in the same way.

sections.title: 1. State the unwanted result
sections.html: Describe what happens now and where it appears in the system. Separate symptoms from constraints you know are real.

sections.title: 2. Write the contradiction
sections.html: Express the conflict as two requirements: what must improve and what must not become worse. Add the condition under which each requirement matters.

sections.title: 3. Separate, redesign, and check
sections.html: Ask whether the requirements can be separated by time, place, condition, component, role, or state. Use a small reversible check and inspect side effects so the conflict is not merely moved elsewhere.

aida-message-optimizer.title: Use AIDA as a Message Clarity Checklist
aida-message-optimizer.subtitle: Make the message relevant, understandable, honest, and actionable.
aida-message-optimizer.description: Check whether a message earns attention, makes the relevant point understandable, explains why it matters, and gives the reader a clear next action without treating AIDA as a persuasion guarantee.
aida-message-optimizer.reason: Replace unsupported response-rate improvements, fabricated A/B outcomes, and formula-like persuasion claims with a bounded editing checklist.
forbidden_public_fragments: Research shows habits can take 21-66 days to form

lifeOsSource.hack: Use Attention, Interest, Desire, and Action as four editing questions, not as a promise that a message will persuade.
lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: Name the audience and desired next step, review the opening for relevance, remove information that does not help understanding, explain the concrete value or consequence honestly, and end with one clear action the reader can accept, decline, or ignore.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: Can the reader quickly tell why this matters, what is being asked, and what they should do next without exaggerated claims or hidden pressure?

faq.question: What matters more than a clever hook?
faq.answer: Relevance. The opening should help the intended reader recognize the problem, decision, or value without hiding the point behind theatrics.

intro.html: AIDA can be used as four editing questions rather than a sales formula. The goal is not to force persuasion. It is to make the message easier to recognize, understand, evaluate, and act on.

sections.title: 1. Attention and interest: relevance first
sections.html: Start with the reader's actual problem, context, decision, or desired result. Give only the context needed to understand the proposal and prefer concrete language over generic hooks.

sections.title: 2. Desire: explain value without overclaiming
sections.html: Describe the plausible benefit, avoided cost, or consequence and the conditions attached to it. Do not invent proof, testimonials, scarcity, or certain outcomes.

sections.title: 3. Action: ask for one clear next step
sections.html: State what the reader can do next and what commitment it implies. Keep the action proportional to the information available and make refusal or deferral possible when appropriate.

attention-to-detail-trainer.title: Run a Detail Check Before You Ship
attention-to-detail-trainer.subtitle: Turn vague carefulness into a bounded verification routine.
attention-to-detail-trainer.description: Inspect a concrete artifact against a small checklist, run a second pass from a different angle, log anomalies, and improve the checklist from real misses rather than training vague hypervigilance.
attention-to-detail-trainer.reason: Replace unsupported perception statistics, fabricated improvement timelines, invented pilot outcomes, and people-observation prompts with a bounded artifact verification routine.
forbidden_public_fragments: Research shows habits can take 21-66 days to form

lifeOsSource.hack: Improve detail work by checking a real artifact against explicit failure modes, not by trying to notice everything.
lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: Choose an artifact or environment where errors matter, write a short checklist from known failure modes, inspect once for completeness and once from a different perspective such as data consistency or user flow, record anomalies, fix them, and update the checklist when a new recurring miss appears.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: What defect or ambiguity did the check find, which checklist item caught it, and what recurring miss should change the next review?

faq.question: Should I try to notice more details everywhere?
faq.answer: No. Use attention where the cost of an error justifies it. A bounded checklist is more actionable than staying continuously alert.

intro.html: Attention to detail is easier to improve when the target is explicit. Instead of trying to become generally hyper-observant, define the failure modes that matter for a specific artifact and build a short verification loop around them.

sections.title: 1. Define what can go wrong
sections.html: Choose a document, dataset, screen, configuration, report, package, or other artifact. List the few mistakes that would create real rework, confusion, or risk.

sections.title: 2. Run two different passes
sections.html: First check the known failure modes systematically. Then change perspective: follow the user flow, reconcile totals, trace links, compare source and output, or inspect naming consistency.

sections.title: 3. Learn from actual misses
sections.html: Log meaningful defects and near-misses. Add a checklist item only when it catches a recurring class of error; remove checks that create noise without changing quality or decisions.

automate-routine-data-reports.title: Automate a Routine Report with Validation and Fallback
automate-routine-data-reports.subtitle: Automate the data path, not hidden judgment.
automate-routine-data-reports.description: Automate a stable reporting workflow only after defining source ownership, transformations, validation rules, freshness, failure handling, and a manual fallback.
automate-routine-data-reports.reason: Replace fabricated team savings, unsupported reliability targets, arbitrary engineering thresholds, and broad automation claims with a bounded report-automation readiness and control protocol.
forbidden_public_fragments: Research shows habits can take 21-66 days to form

lifeOsSource.hack: Automate a report only when the data path and failure behavior are explicit enough to validate.
lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: Map the report consumer, source data, transformations and delivery step. Define validation rules for schema, completeness, freshness and key totals. Build a small automated path with logging and a visible failure state, keep a manual fallback, and stop publication when validation fails.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: Did the automated report use the expected source, pass validation, arrive on time, and fail visibly when an assumption broke?

faq.question: What should happen when validation fails?
faq.answer: Fail visibly, preserve the last trustworthy state where appropriate, notify the owner, and use the manual fallback or repair path. Do not silently publish a result that no longer meets the contract.

intro.html: A report is not ready for automation merely because someone repeats it. Reliable automation needs an explicit data contract, validation, ownership, failure behavior, and a way to recover when an assumption changes.

sections.title: 1. Map the report contract
sections.html: Name the consumer, purpose, source systems, transformation logic, output, schedule, and owner. Mark manual judgments separately rather than hiding them inside code.

sections.title: 2. Define validation before automation
sections.html: Choose checks that would catch a wrong or stale report: expected schema, entity coverage, freshness, reconciled totals, duplicate rules, and important business constraints.

sections.title: 3. Build a visible failure and recovery path
sections.html: Log the run, surface validation failures, and stop or quarantine publication when the contract is broken. Assign an owner and preserve a manual recovery path.
